Ray-Cast Style Voxel Filling determines the interior of a mesh by casting rays along the +Z axis through a pre-classified surface grid and marking voxels as solid when they intersect an outward-facing triangle [S1, unofficial][S2].

The claim states that the method marks voxels as solid when they intersect an 'outward-facing triangle'. However, Source [S1] explicitly states that a voxel is marked as solid if the dot product of the intersection normal and the ray direction is positive (i.e., the normal points in the same direction as the ray, which is +Z). In standard mesh conventions, a normal pointing in the direction of the viewing ray (outward from the viewer) typically indicates an 'inward-facing' or 'back-facing' surface relative to the object's exterior, or simply a surface facing the camera. More importantly, Source [S2] describes a completely different algorithm based on scanning for 'front-facing' and 'back-facing' voxels to fill intervals, not ray-casting against triangle normals in the manner described in the claim. The claim conflates or misrepresents the specific logic found in S1 (which checks for normals aligned with the ray, effectively finding the 'back' of the mesh from the +Z perspective to fill the interior behind it) and ignores the distinct logic in S2. Furthermore, the term 'outward-facing' is ambiguous and often refers to normals pointing away from the object center, whereas the code checks for normals aligned with the +Z axis. The claim's description of the mechanism ('marking voxels as solid when they intersect an outward-facing triangle') is not accurately supported by the evidence which describes marking voxels based on the normal's alignment with the ray direction (finding the first hit from the +Z side, which is technically the 'back' face of the mesh if the mesh is closed and viewed from +Z, or the 'front' face if the mesh is open). Given the discrepancy in the definition of 'outward-facing' vs the code's logic (normal dot ray > 0) and the existence of a different algorithm in S2, the claim is not fully supported.
